A commune is a group of people who choose to live together, share their resources, and run their lives cooperatively. It goes far beyond simply being neighbors. People in a commune don't just happen to live near each other — they actively and intentionally pool what they have (land, money, food, labor) and make decisions together, as a group.

Think of it this way: in a regular neighborhood, you own your house, earn your own money, cook your own meals, and mind your own business. In a commune, the boundaries between "mine" and "ours" are blurred on purpose. What belongs to the group belongs to everyone in it.

The word "commune" carries two distinct but related meanings depending on context.

1. A Close-Knit Community Built on Shared Living

This is the meaning most people think of first in everyday English. A commune is a group — sometimes a few families, sometimes dozens of people — who deliberately set up a life together around shared values and shared ownership.

Key features almost always include:

  • Shared property: Land, buildings, tools, and often money are held collectively, not individually.
  • Shared work: Tasks like farming, cooking, childcare, and building are divided among members so everyone contributes.
  • Shared decision-making: The group governs itself, usually through open discussion and group agreement rather than a single leader having all the power.
  • A unifying belief or philosophy: Most communes form around something the members deeply believe in — it could be a religion, a political idea (like socialism), a lifestyle philosophy (like environmentalism or simple living), or a spiritual practice.

Real-world examples:

  • In the 1960s and 1970s, especially in the United States, thousands of communes were formed by young people who rejected mainstream consumer society. They moved to rural areas, grew their own food, shared everything, and tried to build an alternative way of life. These are often called hippie communes.
  • The Hutterites are a Christian religious group who have lived in agricultural communes for centuries across North America. They own everything collectively, work together, and eat together in communal dining halls.
  • Kibbutzim (plural of kibbutz) in Israel are a famous form of commune where members historically shared all property and income, farming the land together. Many still operate today, though some have become less strictly collective over time.
  • Modern eco-communes or intentional communities bring people together around environmental values — living sustainably, growing food organically, minimizing waste — as a shared mission.

What all of these have in common is the intention behind the arrangement. A commune doesn't happen by accident. People choose it because they believe that living collectively is better — morally, practically, or spiritually — than living individualistically.

2. A Unit of Local Government (Administrative Meaning)

In several European countries — most notably France, but also Belgium, Switzerland, Luxembourg, and others — a "commune" is simply the smallest official unit of government. It's roughly what you'd call a municipality or township in English.

France, for instance, is divided into thousands of communes (around 35,000 of them). Each commune, whether it's a tiny village of 50 people or a large city, has its own elected local government led by a mayor (maire). The commune handles local matters: roads, local taxes, public spaces, and so on.

In this sense, the word carries no special social or ideological weight. It's a neutral administrative label, the way "county" or "district" is in English. A French person saying their commune is "Saint-Rémy-de-Provence" is simply stating where they officially live — the equivalent of saying "I live in the township of Springfield."

This meaning also appears in other parts of the world influenced by French administrative traditions, including parts of Africa and South America.
A Famous Historical Example: The Paris Commune

No explanation of this word is complete without mentioning the Paris Commune of 1871. After France was defeated in the Franco-Prussian War, the people of Paris briefly seized control of the city and established their own self-governing revolutionary government, which they called "the Commune." It lasted only about two months (March to May 1871) before being violently crushed by the French national government.

The Paris Commune became enormously important in political history because it was seen as an early real-world experiment in radical, worker-led self-governance. Political thinkers — especially Marxists and socialists — studied it intensely. It gave the word "commune" a strong association with ideas of collective power, workers' rights, and anti-establishment governance that lingered for generations.
How It Differs from Similar Words

It helps to understand what a commune is not, by comparing it to nearby words:

  • A community is broad and loose. It just means people who share something — a neighborhood, an interest, an identity. There's no implication of shared property or deliberate cooperation. A commune is always a community, but a community is not always a commune.
  • A neighborhood is purely geographical. People live near each other, but they own their own homes, live their own separate lives, and have no obligation to cooperate economically or socially.
  • A cooperative (or co-op) involves shared ownership of something specific — a grocery store, a housing building, a farm — but members don't necessarily live together or share all aspects of life.
  • A collective is similar in spirit to a commune but often refers more specifically to a group organized around a shared work or business activity, rather than a whole shared way of life.

A commune is the most total and immersive of these concepts. It's not just about sharing one thing. It's about sharing life itself.
The Word's Connotations in Modern English

When English speakers use the word "commune" today, it often carries a mildly idealistic or countercultural flavor. It tends to evoke images of people who have stepped away from mainstream society to try something different. Depending on who is using the word and how, it can sound:

  • Admiring — suggesting a brave, principled, back-to-basics way of life.
  • Neutral — simply describing a type of organized community.
  • Skeptical or dismissive — implying that the people involved are naïve, impractical, or out of touch.

The word itself doesn't carry any of these judgments built in. Context and tone do the work.

A commune (noun) is either:

  1. A group of people who have chosen to live together and share property, work, and decision-making around a common set of values or beliefs — the most total form of cooperative living there is.
  2. The smallest unit of local government in France and several other countries — a neutral administrative term for a municipality.

The social meaning (shared community living) is the one most commonly encountered in English. The administrative meaning is the one most commonly encountered in the context of French or European governance. Both meanings share the same underlying spirit: a commune is not just a place, but a group of people bound together by more than geography — bound by shared responsibility and shared life.
